title: Viral warts (HPV)
summary: Benign HPV-driven epidermal growths. Most clear on their own. Salicylic acid is the community first line, cryotherapy is clinic-based, and refer the immunosuppressed and anything atypical.

glance.think: A rough, hyperkeratotic papule with black dots (thrombosed capillaries) that interrupts the skin lines, on hands, feet or around the nails.
glance.engine: Cutaneous HPV infects basal keratinocytes and causes hyperkeratosis. Spread is by contact, fomites and autoinoculation.
glance.backbone: Reassure (many resolve), or salicylic acid daily after paring for 8–12 weeks, with or without cryotherapy.
glance.never_miss: A rapidly growing or ulcerating ‘wart’, especially in an immunosuppressed patient, may be SCC. Refer.

what: Viral warts (verrucae) are very common **benign** growths of the epidermis caused by cutaneous **human papillomavirus (HPV)**. This page covers **cutaneous** warts. Anogenital warts belong to sexual health and are counselled separately.

list: HPV is a double-stranded DNA virus. Common cutaneous types are **1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 27, 29 and 57**.
It infects **basal keratinocytes**, producing hyperkeratosis and new virus particles.
Spread is by skin-to-skin contact, fomites (swimming pools, changing rooms), and **autoinoculation**. A line of warts along a scratch is the pseudo-Koebner phenomenon.
Incubation takes weeks to months. The wart burden is higher with dermatitis or **immunosuppression** (transplant, HIV).

head: Type
Features
Sites
rows: Rough hyperkeratotic papules; black or red dots are thrombosed capillaries
Inward-growing and painful (myrmecia), or clustered ‘mosaic’ warts; **interrupt the skin lines**
Flat-topped, skin-coloured, often numerous; spread by shaving
Thin fronds on a narrow base
Around or under the nail; risk of nail dystrophy

list: **Clinical.** Paring reveals pinpoint bleeding or black dots. Dermoscopy helps.
**Plantar wart vs corn:** a wart is tender when **squeezed from the sides**. A corn is tender on **direct pressure**, and the skin lines run through it.
**Biopsy** if SCC is a concern, especially in immunosuppressed patients.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: At a pressure site; skin lines continue through it; no capillary dots
Rapid growth, ulceration or tenderness, often in an older or immunosuppressed patient. **Refer**

management: Many warts **resolve without treatment**: roughly half of childhood warts within 6 months, and most within 2 years. Treat if they are painful, disabling, in an immunosuppressed patient, or if the patient prefers.

list: **Salicylic acid** paint, gel or plaster **daily**. Soak and pare (or file) first. Persist for **8–12 weeks**. Protect the surrounding skin, and avoid in diabetes or neuropathy with poor sensation.

**Cryotherapy** (liquid nitrogen) is clinic-based and needs repeated sessions. It can blister and hurt, and may cause hypo- or hyperpigmentation (more so in skin of colour). Take care over superficial nerves.

management: Curettage or electrosurgery (scarring risk), radiofrequency cautery, CO₂ laser, intralesional bleomycin, contact immunotherapy (e.g. diphencyprone), microwave (plantar), and podophyllin or imiquimod (better evidence for anogenital than cutaneous warts).
red_flags: Rapid growth, bleeding, ulceration or an atypical appearance: consider **SCC** and refer.
**Immunosuppressed** patient (transplant, HIV) with extensive or recalcitrant warts: refer to dermatology.
Extensive facial or periungual warts where destructive treatment risks scarring or nail damage.
Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy or vascular disease: avoid self-treatment with salicylic acid or cryotherapy on the feet.
pearls: No treatment ‘kills’ HPV instantly. Treatment removes virus-bearing skin, and recurrence is common until immunity clears that type.
Duct-tape occlusion has mixed evidence. It is an optional add-on, not a cure.
Periungual warts: avoid aggressive destruction near the **nail matrix**.
Advise flip-flops in communal showers, not sharing towels, and covering verrucae for swimming.
